prompt: Where does most of a SOAR playbook's value come from, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Replacing the SIEM's correlation rules
choices.why: The SIEM raises the alert; the playbook starts from it.

choices.text: Responding faster than any person could, by taking the decision away from the analyst on duty
choices.why: Speed helps, but the lesson places the decision with a person in most cases.

choices.text: Writing the incident report automatically at the end
choices.why: A ticket is a record, not the report of lesson 20.

choices.text: Gathering the same facts every time
choices.why: Right. Enrichment, done the same way without forgetting a step.

prompt: Match each step to how the lesson's five questions judge it.

pairs.left: looking up how often an address failed

pairs.right: a person decides and does it

prompt: Why does disabling an employee's account fail the lesson's test for automation?

choices.text: It happens too rarely to be worth writing down
choices.why: Frequency is not the problem here.

choices.text: It stops somebody's work, and the right call depends on who they are
choices.why: Right. It needs judgement and it is wide for the person it hits.

choices.text: Directories have no interface a playbook could call
choices.why: They do; the obstacle is judgement, not plumbing.

choices.text: It cannot be undone once done, since a disabled account loses its files and settings for good
choices.why: An account can be re-enabled; the harm is the interruption.

prompt: Order the five parts of a playbook.
A team is about to switch on its first playbook. In what order does the lesson suggest removing approvals?

choices.text: Start with every action approved, and remove approval one action at a time when the record justifies it
choices.why: Right. Trust is earned per action, from measurements.

choices.text: Approve nothing for low alerts and everything for critical ones
choices.why: Severity of the alert is not the measure of the action's risk.

choices.text: Keep approval forever on every action
choices.why: Possible, but the lesson describes how it can be earned away.

choices.text: Start fully automatic, and add approval wherever a mistake happens
choices.why: That learns from the outages it causes.

prompt: Why does the playbook write a ticket even when it decides to do nothing?
hint: What does silence look like from outside?

choices.text: A silent run looks the same as a failed one
choices.why: Right. The record is what tells the two apart.

choices.text: To keep the approver's name in the firewall's comment
choices.why: The firewall comment is written only when it acts.

choices.text: The SIEM deletes alerts that have no ticket attached
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson's SIEM does that.

choices.text: The law requires a ticket for every alert
choices.why: No law in this course says so.

prompt: Over how many distinct accounts did 203.0.113.66 fail, according to the playbook?
hint: The first line of its output.

prompt: The playbook blocked the address but only proposed disabling bruno. Why the difference?
hint: One of them stops a person's work.

choices.text: ana did not approve the second action
choices.why: She approved the run; the playbook never offers that action.

choices.text: A person has to check first whether bruno himself also logged in that morning
choices.why: Right. Blocking one outside address is narrow and reversible; the account decision needs judgement.

choices.text: Accounts live on gw and the playbook only reaches fw
choices.why: Reach is not the reason; the lesson's table is.

choices.text: bruno's account is on the never-block list
choices.why: That list holds addresses, not accounts.

prompt: What does the comment on the firewall rule record?

choices.text: Who approved it
choices.why: Right. `playbook, approved by ana`.

choices.text: The time the alert fired
choices.why: The ticket holds times; the comment holds the approver.

choices.text: The rule's handle
choices.why: nft assigns the handle; the comment is the playbook's text.

choices.text: The number of failed logins
choices.why: That is in the ticket.

prompt: What would have happened had the playbook blocked 203.0.113.150 at night with no guard?

choices.text: Nothing, since the provider only sends and never receives
choices.why: files sends to it; blocking it stops the backup.

choices.text: Staff working from home could not reach gw
choices.why: Staff use their own addresses, not the provider's.

choices.text: The SIEM would raise an alert for the block
choices.why: No rule watches for that in this lesson.

choices.text: The nightly backup would have failed, and nobody would know
choices.why: Right. Automation fails quickly and with confidence; the never-block list exists for this.

choices.text: nftables refuses rules that block private address ranges like this one
choices.why: They can; the playbook chooses not to.

choices.text: ana's approval was missing
choices.why: She approved; the guard refused anyway.

choices.text: It had no failed logins
choices.why: The guard does not look at failures.

choices.text: It is inside one of the company's own networks
choices.why: Right. An automated action against its own infrastructure is refused.

prompt: When should the undo for a playbook's action be written and tested?
hint: Not at three in the morning.

choices.text: After the first time it blocks the wrong address, when the need is clear
choices.why: That is when it is needed, which is too late to write it.

choices.text: During the lessons-learned meeting, with the whole team present
choices.why: Lesson 15's meeting is after the damage.

choices.text: Only for actions that touch accounts
choices.why: Every action needs one.

choices.text: Before the playbook's first run
choices.why: Right. An action you cannot reverse quickly belongs to a person.

prompt: A production playbook counts its own actions per hour and stops when the count looks like a flood. This guardrail is called a ___ limit.
hint: How many per unit of time.

prompt: In the worked example, an alert fires at 02:35 and a person takes it at 08:12. How many minutes is that interval?
Rules get better and alerts fire seconds after each event, but incidents still take hours to contain. Which measure is the problem?
hint: Between the alert and a person.

choices.text: MTTD
choices.why: Detection is the part that improved.

choices.text: The rule's level
choices.why: A level is not a time measure.

choices.text: The share of overruled proposals
choices.why: That measures the playbook's judgement, not the wait.

choices.text: MTTA
choices.why: Right. Detection is fast; the wait for somebody to take the alert is the gap.

prompt: On Thursday's worked example, what would have cut the response time the most?

choices.text: Running the rule every minute instead of every five
choices.why: That shaves detection by minutes; the wait was hours.

choices.text: Letting the playbook block without approval
choices.why: That saves the minutes after 08:12, not the hours before.

choices.text: Sending the critical alert to a phone at 02:35, with the ticket attached
choices.why: Right. Five and a half hours were waiting; the playbook saved minutes.

choices.text: A faster computer for the SIEM
choices.why: The SIEM was not the slow part.

prompt: A broken rule starts raising 300 alerts an hour for different addresses, all approved by a sleepy analyst clicking through. Which guardrail stops the damage?
hint: Approval is already there, and failing.

choices.text: The comment with the approver's name
choices.why: It says who; it limits nothing.

choices.text: A rate limit that stops the playbook and tells somebody
choices.why: Right. Approval only helps if it is read; a count per hour does not get tired.

choices.text: The never-block list
choices.why: It protects named addresses, not against volume.

choices.text: The ticket written on each run, which a manager reviews the next morning to reverse the wrong blocks
choices.why: It records the damage; it does not stop it.

prompt: What does the lesson say decides when an approval step may be removed from a playbook?

choices.text: Whether the vendor recommends it
choices.why: The lesson argues from your own record.

choices.text: How fast it runs
choices.why: Speed is not correctness.

choices.text: How many of its proposals a person overruled
choices.why: Right. A low share, measured over many runs, earns trust.

choices.text: How many alerts it has handled in total since the team switched it on
choices.why: Volume alone says nothing about being right.
